docs.title: Now That They Can Find You, How Do You Charge Them?
docs.text:
Chapter 13 got your message and offer in front of real customers. This chapter fills in the Revenue block: exactly how the venture turns that attention into actual money — not just how much to charge, but how the charging itself is structured.

Turning Attention Into Income

A customer finding you is only useful if it eventually turns into money you can count on. This chapter is about designing exactly how that happens. Let's find out for real!

docs.title: What Is a Revenue Model
docs.text:
A revenue model is the overall structure describing how a venture generates income from its offer — not a specific dollar amount, but the pattern by which money flows in at all. A revenue model is built from one or more revenue streams: distinct sources of income within the venture, which may come from different offers, different customer segments, or different pricing arrangements for the same core offer.

Every revenue stream takes one of two basic shapes. Recurring revenue is income collected repeatedly from the same customer on an ongoing basis — a subscription renewing every month. Transaction revenue is income collected once per discrete purchase, with no ongoing commitment from the customer — Jordan's $40-per-session model is transaction revenue; a hypothetical monthly grooming plan would be recurring revenue instead.

docs.title: Choosing a Pricing Model
docs.text:
With a revenue stream shape chosen, a founder selects a pricing model: the specific structure by which a price is set and charged to the customer, distinct from the revenue model's broader income pattern. That choice is guided by a pricing strategy: the reasoning behind why a particular pricing model was chosen, tied back to the target customer, the value proposition, and the competitive landscape from earlier chapters.

Pricing Model How It Works Best Fit Subscription Pricing Customer pays a fixed amount on a recurring schedule Ongoing needs, recurring revenue One-Time Pricing Customer pays once for a single transaction Occasional needs, transaction revenue Tiered Pricing Customer chooses among several price/feature levels Customers with different needs or budgets Freemium Model A basic version is free; paid tiers unlock more Digital offers where free access can build a paying base

Subscription pricing charges the customer a fixed amount on a recurring schedule in exchange for ongoing access. One-time pricing charges the customer a single amount for a single transaction, with no ongoing commitment on either side. Tiered pricing offers the same core solution at multiple price and feature levels, letting customers self-select based on their own needs and budget. A freemium model offers a basic version of a solution for free, while charging for a premium tier with additional features — a structure best suited to digital or software offers where serving a free user costs the venture very little.

The Pricing Model Shapes Behavior, Not Just Revenue

Notice that the pricing model isn't just about how much money arrives — it shapes how customers behave. Subscription pricing rewards a founder for keeping customers happy every single month. One-time pricing rewards a founder for making each individual transaction excellent. Choosing a model means choosing which behavior you want to be rewarded for.

docs.title: Two Ways to Set a Price
docs.text: Once a model is chosen, an actual number still has to be set. Value-based pricing sets the price according to how much value the customer believes they're receiving — grounded in the benefit articulated back in Chapter 8 — rather than in what the offer costs to deliver. Cost-plus pricing sets the price by starting from what the offer costs to deliver and adding a fixed margin on top, guaranteeing profitability on paper but ignoring what the customer would actually be willing to pay. Jordan's $40 driveway price emerged from value-based thinking — anchored to what customers said driving to a groomer already cost them in lost time — rather than from simply totaling up supply costs and adding a margin.

docs.title: Testing Your Price Like Everything Else
docs.text:
A price, like every other canvas block, starts as a revenue assumption: an unverified belief about what a customer will pay and how often, which needs the same field-tested treatment as every assumption since Chapter 1. That belief centers on willingness to pay: the actual maximum amount a specific customer would pay for a specific offer, which can only be discovered through real behavior, not guessed from a survey question. Price point testing is the lean test, following the same principles from Chapter 10, of offering the same or similar offer at different prices to different customers to observe how willingness to pay actually changes. Pricing validation is confirming, through real transactions rather than opinions, that a chosen price point produces enough paying customers to sustain the venture.

Test Two Prices at Once, on Different People

Here's a shortcut for price point testing: offer $35 to one group of prospective customers and $45 to another, at the same time. Comparing how many say yes at each price tells you far more about willingness to pay than asking anyone directly what they'd be willing to spend.

docs.title: Projecting Revenue and Finding Break-Even
docs.text:
With a validated price in hand, a founder can start doing real math. A revenue projection is an estimate of future income, built from real evidence — actual price points, actual test results — rather than optimistic guessing. Central to that estimate is sales conversion: the rate at which people who show interest actually become paying customers, measured directly from field test results like the ones from Chapter 10. Break-even thinking is the discipline of calculating the point at which total revenue exactly covers total costs, so a founder knows precisely how many sales are needed before the venture stops losing money on each period.

Before trying the calculator below, notice that break-even depends on three numbers working together: price, cost per sale, and fixed monthly costs — change any one, and the number of sales needed to break even shifts too.

docs.title: Diagram: Break-Even Calculator
docs.text:
Break-Even Calculator

Type: microsim sim-id: break-even-calculator Library: p5.js Status: Specified

Bloom Level: Apply (L3) Bloom Verb: calculate

Learning objective: Learners adjust price, per-sale cost, and fixed monthly cost sliders and calculate how many sales are needed to reach break-even for a lean venture.

Canvas layout:

  • Three sliders, top to bottom: "Price per Sale" (\(10-\)100), "Cost per Sale" (\(0-\)50), "Fixed Monthly Costs" (\(0-\)500)
  • Below: a live-updating result reading "Sales Needed to Break Even This Month: N"
  • A simple bar showing current monthly sales (a 4th slider, "Sales This Month," 0-30) against the break-even line

Behavior: Break-even sales = Fixed Monthly Costs / (Price per Sale − Cost per Sale). Recalculate and redraw on every slider change. If Price per Sale ≤ Cost per Sale, display a warning message: "At this price, you can never break even — raise the price or lower the cost." The bar chart shows a red bar if "Sales This Month" is below the break-even number, green if at or above it.

Interactive controls:

  • Drag any of the 4 sliders; all outputs update live
  • "Load Jordan's Numbers" button sets Price=\(40, Cost per Sale=\)8, Fixed Monthly Costs=$120, Sales This Month=5

Default parameters: Price=\(40, Cost per Sale=\)8, Fixed Monthly Costs=$120, Sales This Month=0 (so the bar starts red, prompting exploration).

Implementation notes: Use p5.js. Recompute break-even on every draw() call from current slider values; guard the division against Price equal to Cost per Sale. Must remain fully usable on narrow (mobile) viewports — stack sliders vertically with the result and bar chart below.

Don't Build a Revenue Projection on Hope

A common trap here is projecting revenue from an imagined future conversion rate instead of a measured one. The fix: use the actual sales conversion rate from your Chapter 10 lean tests, even if it's a small, humble number — a revenue projection built on real evidence is worth far more than an optimistic guess, even a modest one.

docs.title: Communicating Your Price
docs.text: The final piece connects straight back to Chapter 12. Pricing communication is how a price gets presented to the customer — clearly, honestly, and without hidden terms — using the same message clarity and simplicity principles that govern every other piece of customer-facing language.

docs.title: Key Takeaways
docs.text:
Before Chapter 15 turns to what the venture needs to spend, hold onto how money comes in:

  • A revenue model is built from one or more revenue streams, shaped as recurring revenue or transaction revenue.
  • A pricing model — subscription, one-time, tiered pricing, or a freemium model — is chosen according to a deliberate pricing strategy, then priced using value-based pricing or cost-plus pricing.
  • Every price starts as a revenue assumption about willingness to pay, tested through price point testing and confirmed by pricing validation.
  • A real revenue projection, grounded in measured sales conversion, supports honest break-even thinking — and the final price reaches the customer through clear pricing communication.

You Just Designed How Money Actually Flows In

You now have a revenue model and a validated price — grounded in real willingness to pay, not a guess. Let's find out for real, starting with what the venture needs to spend in Chapter 15.

docs.title: Subject & Tone

docs.title: Title

docs.title: Why This Mascot
docs.text: A fox is clever, resourceful, and agile — exactly the qualities the course asks of a founder testing an idea against real-world friction rather than building in isolation, and fox-orange fur pairs naturally with the book's Material "orange" accent color. The name Scout ties the mascot directly to the course's signature pedagogical device, the "Field Discovery Window," so the character's very identity reinforces the course's most distinctive teaching method: get out and talk to real customers.

docs.title: Learning Graph for The Eight-Hour Entrepreneur
docs.text:
This section contains the learning graph for this textbook. A learning graph is a graph of concepts used in this textbook. Each concept is represented by a node in a network graph. Concepts are connected by directed edges that indicate what concepts each node depends on before that concept is understood by the student.

A learning graph is the foundational data structure for intelligent textbooks that can recommend learning paths. A learning graph is like a roadmap of concepts to help students arrive at their learning goals.

At the left of the learning graph are prerequisite or foundational concepts. They have no outbound edges. They only have inbound edges for other concepts that depend on understanding these foundational prerequisite concepts. At the far right we have the most advanced concepts in the course. To master these concepts you must understand all the concepts that they point to.

Here are other files used by the learning graph.

docs.title: Course Description
docs.text: We use the Course Description as the source document for the concepts that are included in this course. The course description uses the 2001 Bloom taxonomy to order learning objectives.

docs.title: List of Concepts
docs.text: We use generative AI to convert the course description into a Concept List. Each concept is in the form of a short Title Case label with most labels under 32 characters long.

docs.title: Concept Dependency List
docs.text: We next use generative AI to create a Directed Acyclic Graph (DAG). DAGs do not have cycles where concepts depend on themselves. We provide the DAG in two formats. One is a CSV file and the other format is a JSON file that uses the vis-network JavaScript library format. The vis-network format uses nodes, edges and metadata elements with edges containing from and to properties. This makes it easy for you to view and edit the learning graph using an editor built with the vis-network tools.

docs.title: Concept Taxonomy
docs.text: The 300 concepts in the learning graph are organized into 14 categories, each evenly distributed (no category exceeds 10% of the total) and mapped to the course's week-by-week structure and the CO.STARTERS Canvas framework.

docs.title: FOUND — Entrepreneurship Foundations & Philosophy
docs.text: The mindset, vocabulary, and course philosophy underlying the whole program: what an early-stage venture is, the idea trap, the Clarity → Validation → Action → Launch philosophy, and the psychological-safety norms of the cohort.

docs.title: CANV — CO.STARTERS Canvas Framework
docs.text: The Business Model Canvas adaptation used throughout the course and its 11 individual blocks (Customer, Problem, Solution, Alternatives, Benefit, Advantage, Message, Distribution, Revenue, Startup Needs, Costs).

docs.title: CUST — Customer Discovery & Segmentation
docs.text: Identifying and defining who the venture serves: target customer, personas, market segments, and customer prioritization.

docs.title: PROB — Problem Definition & Pain Points
docs.text: Defining the real problem a customer has: pain points, root causes, problem severity/frequency, and problem validation.

docs.title: SOL — Solution Design & Offer Development
docs.text: Framing what is offered to solve the validated problem: initial offer, minimum viable offer, and solution iteration.

docs.title: ALT — Alternatives & Competitive Analysis
docs.text: How customers currently solve the problem: competitors, workarounds, substitutes, and competitive positioning.

docs.title: VALU — Value Proposition: Benefit & Advantage
docs.text: Why the customer wants the solution and why this founder is positioned to deliver it: benefit, advantage, and value-proposition articulation.

docs.title: INTV — Discovery Interviews & Research Methods
docs.text: Techniques for talking to real customers: interview design, the Reality Check pressure test, and synthesizing findings.

docs.title: VALID — Lean Validation & Testing
docs.text: Testing assumptions cheaply before building: lean tests, pre-selling, manual service delivery, and kill/pivot/persevere decisions.

docs.title: MSG — Messaging & Communication
docs.text: Turning a validated concept into clear, compelling communication: value-proposition statements, sales copy, and founder narrative.

docs.title: DIST — Distribution & Go-to-Market
docs.text: How the product or service reaches the customer: channel selection, word of mouth, and multi-channel strategy.

docs.title: REV — Revenue Models & Pricing
docs.text: How the venture makes money: pricing models, pricing validation, and willingness to pay.

docs.title: FIN — Startup Needs & Cost Planning
docs.text: One-time startup needs versus ongoing costs, and basic financial-planning literacy for a lean venture.

docs.title: LAUNCH — Launch Planning, Pitching & Accountability
docs.text: Synthesizing the canvas into a 30-day launch roadmap, pitching to peers, and the accountability structures that sustain momentum after the course.

docs.title: Gap Analysis
docs.text:
Only one element scored below full points:

  • Descriptive Context (4/5): The Course Overview section explains the course's purpose and value well, but the sentence "The course operationalize a core philosophy..." and "how the Field Discovery Window operationalize real-world validation" both have a subject–verb agreement error (should be "operationalizes"). This is a proofreading issue, not a content gap — it doesn't affect learning graph generation.

Every other rubric element is fully satisfied. No structural gaps exist that would limit concept extraction.

docs.title: Improvement Suggestions
docs.text:
1. Proofread the Course Overview section — fix "operationalize" → "operationalizes" in both occurrences (paragraph 2 of Course Overview, and the Understand-level outcome about the Field Discovery Window). Low priority; purely cosmetic.
  2. Optional, not required for readiness: consider adding 1–2 explicit outcomes tied to peer accountability / cohort dynamics (e.g., "Explain how public commitment and peer feedback increase follow-through on the 30-day launch plan") — the course overview and Week 4 syllabus emphasize this heavily but it's currently only implicit in the outcomes.

docs.title: Concept Generation Readiness
docs.text:
The course description is well-suited to generating 200+ concepts:

  • 16 main topics, each mapping to a CO.STARTERS Canvas block or a discrete workshop activity (interviews, pressure test, lean testing, messaging, pricing, launch planning) — each topic alone can reasonably decompose into 8–15 concepts (definitions, techniques, examples, common pitfalls), suggesting 150–200+ concepts from topics alone.
  • 24 Bloom's-Taxonomy outcomes spanning all six levels, each implying distinct procedural or conceptual concepts (e.g., "pressure test," "lean validation test," "minimum testable iteration," "value proposition," "Startup Needs vs. Costs") that expand the topic-derived concept pool further.
  • The explicit Topics Not Covered section keeps scope bounded, which will help the learning-graph-generator avoid concept drift into adjacent domains (e.g., accounting, fundraising) that aren't part of this course.

Estimate: sufficient depth and breadth to reach the ~200-concept target without artificial padding.

docs.title: MicroSims
docs.text:
MicroSims are small, interactive educational simulations — each one focused on a single concept. They live under docs/sims/<sim-name>/ and are embedded into chapters via iframes.

New MicroSims can be created with the microsim-generator skill, which routes to the appropriate library (p5.js, Chart.js, vis-network, Mermaid, Leaflet, Plotly, Venn.js).

docs.title: Assumption Ledger Sorter
docs.text: Run the Assumption Ledger Sorter MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
Every business idea starts out built entirely from assumptions. The skill this MicroSim practices is telling the difference between a statement someone has actually tested and one that only sounds true.

Learners work through six cards from Jordan's ledger, the running list of beliefs and findings behind Jordan's mobile dog-grooming idea. For each card they choose Assumption or Validated Learning. The feedback is immediate:

  • A correct answer flashes green; an incorrect answer flashes amber.
  • The correct category is stamped on the card.
  • A one-sentence explanation says why, so a wrong answer still teaches something.

Some cards are deliberately tricky. "2 of 5 neighbors said the price was too high" is validated learning even though it is bad news, and "A mobile service is obviously more convenient" is an assumption even though it sounds reasonable.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Read the statement on the card.
  2. Click Assumption or Validated Learning.
  3. Read the feedback, then click Next Card.
  4. After card 6, click See Results for your score and a review of any cards you missed.
  5. Click Try Again to sort the same six cards in a new, shuffled order.

The progress bar across the top turns green or amber for each card as you go. Nothing is saved; the score lasts only for the current session.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Given short statements from Jordan's dog-grooming-van idea, participants will classify each one as an Assumption (untested) or Validated Learning (tested), applying the chapter's definitions to concrete cases.

Bloom Level: Apply (L3). Bloom Verb: classify.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 5-10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text: • Chapter 1 reading on assumptions and validated learning

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Solo sort (4 min): Each participant sorts all six cards and notes their score.
  2. Debrief the tricky cards (3 min): As a group, discuss cards 4 and 5. Why is bad news still validated learning? Why does "obviously" signal an untested belief?
  3. Sort your own ledger (3 min): Each participant writes three statements about their own idea and labels each one, asking "how do I know this?" for every line.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Did the participant classify at least 5 of 6 cards correctly on a second attempt?
  • Can the participant explain why a customer's "no" counts as validated learning?
  • Can the participant rewrite one of their own assumptions as a test they could run this week?

docs.title: References
docs.text:
1. Lean startup - Wikipedia - Defines validated learning, the category that real customer evidence falls into.
  2. Hypothesis - Wikipedia - An assumption is a business hypothesis that has not been tested yet.
  3. Confirmation bias - Wikipedia - Why statements that "sound obviously true" are easy to mistake for evidence.
  4. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - How to gather customer feedback that counts as real evidence instead of polite opinion.

docs.title: The Four-Phase Founder Pipeline
docs.text: Run the Four-Phase Founder Pipeline MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
This course runs on a four-phase philosophy: Clarity → Validation → Action → Launch. The MicroSim lets participants step through the phases at their own pace instead of watching an animation they cannot pause. Each phase shows three things:

  • What it means: a one-sentence definition of the phase.
  • Jordan's example: what Jordan, the dog-grooming-van founder from Chapter 1, actually did in that phase.
  • Before you click Next: a question that asks the learner to predict the next move before seeing it.

A curved return arrow from Validation back to Clarity, labeled if evidence says pivot, shows that the phases form a cycle. Clicking Next on Launch loops back to Clarity for the same reason: every launch produces new evidence that sharpens the next round.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. The sim opens on Clarity. Read the definition and Jordan's example.
  2. Answer the Before you click Next question in your head (or in the chat), then click Next ▶.
  3. Click any phase box to jump straight to it. ◀ Previous steps back.
  4. Click the curved if evidence says pivot arrow to see why Validation can send you back to Clarity.
  5. On Launch, the Next button becomes Back to Clarity ↺ to show that the cycle repeats.

The left and right arrow keys also step through the phases once the sim has focus. On narrow screens the four boxes stack vertically.

docs.title: Audience
docs.text: Adult early-stage entrepreneurs and aspiring founders in a live virtual cohort.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will be able to explain, in their own words, the purpose of each of the four phases (Clarity, Validation, Action, Launch) and how the phases connect into a repeating cycle rather than a one-time sequence.

Bloom Level: Understand (L2). Bloom Verb: explain.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10-15 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites
docs.text:
• Chapter 1 reading on the Clarity → Validation → Action → Launch philosophy
  • Familiarity with Jordan's mobile dog-grooming example

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Guided walk-through (5 min): The facilitator shares the sim and pauses on each phase. Before each click of Next, participants type their prediction into the chat.
  2. Pivot scenario (3 min): Click the return arrow. Ask: what evidence would send Jordan back to Clarity? What would change in Jordan's one-sentence guess?
  3. Apply to your own idea (5 min): In breakout rooms, each participant writes their own one-line example for Clarity and Validation, using Jordan's examples as a model.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant explain each phase without reading the definition off the screen?
  • Can the participant describe a piece of evidence that would trigger a pivot back to Clarity?
  • Does the participant describe the phases as a cycle rather than a checklist?

  2. Minimum viable product - Wikipedia - The idea behind Jordan's driveway groom: the smallest version that produces real evidence.
  3. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's discovery-and-validation process, including when to pivot.

docs.title: The Idea Trap Cycle
docs.text: Run the Idea Trap Cycle MicroSim Fullscreen Edit in the p5.js Editor

docs.title: About This MicroSim
docs.text:
The idea trap is hard to spot from the inside because it looks like diligence. This MicroSim puts the two ways a founder can spend the next hour side by side. On the left, Unrefined Business Idea and Refine the Plan form a closed loop: pitch decks, logos, and spreadsheets feel like progress, but the arrow always leads back to the same unanswered question. On the right, a straight path runs from the idea to a Real-World Test and ends at Validated Learning, a real answer of yes or no.

The example follows Jordan, the founder from Chapter 1 who wants to drive a dog-grooming van to customers' homes. Two counters make the contrast concrete: Hours invested climbs on both paths, but Real customer answers only moves when Jordan runs a real-world test.

docs.title: How to Use
docs.text:
1. Click any box to read what it means, with Jordan's version of it.
  2. Hover over (or tap) an arrow. The loop and the forward path each explain what kind of path they are.
  3. Click Refine the Plan several times. Watch Jordan circle the loop while hours pile up and customer answers stay at zero.
  4. Click Test with Customers. Jordan moves down the forward path, and each test adds real answers, including answers of "no."
  5. Click Reset to start over.

On narrow screens the loop sits on top and the forward path runs down the right side.

docs.title: Learning Objective
docs.text:
Participants will be able to differentiate productive early-stage activity (real-world testing) from unproductive activity (endless refinement) and recognize when they are personally in the idea trap.

Bloom Level: Analyze (L4). Bloom Verb: differentiate.

docs.title: Duration
docs.text: 10 minutes

docs.title: Prerequisites

  • An unrefined business idea of their own

docs.title: Activities
docs.text:
1. Explore (3 min): Individually, click all four boxes and hover both arrows.
  2. Predict and test (3 min): Before touching the buttons, predict how many times Jordan must click Refine the Plan before the customer-answers counter moves. Then try it, and compare with one click of Test with Customers.
  3. Breakout discussion (4 min): In breakout rooms, each person lists the last three things they did for their own idea and sorts each one onto the loop or the forward path.

docs.title: Assessment
docs.text:
• Can the participant explain why refining a plan never changes the customer-answers count?
  • Can the participant name one "forward path" action they will take before the next session?
  • Does the participant recognize that a "no" from a real customer is still validated learning?

  2. Customer development - Wikipedia - Steve Blank's method of getting out of the building to test assumptions with real customers.
  3. The Mom Test - Rob Fitzpatrick - A practical guide to asking customers questions that produce honest, useful answers.
  4. CO.STARTERS - The entrepreneurship program whose canvas and philosophy this course adapts.
